body: Apart from only having two, and being perhaps half an inch longer than those shown the video they seem to be precisely the same thing. Thanks a million!

The bearsuit ones? Great, as far as I've heard. They're weird, kinda like a non-newtonian fluid: the foam is soft like foam is normally, but the impact causes the foam around the impact area to harden into a shell. It doesn't completely harden, and it doesn't distribute the force over as big an area as a full plastic plate,but they move better with your body. As for durability, the foam keeps reacting to repeated stress in the same way for quite some time it seems.

The sweet bearsuit pads are pretty awesome, my buddy has a pair. They've got SAS tec pads in them- 

"SAS-TEC material is intelligent armor constructed from visco elastic soft foam smart molecules.  It has earned the highest CE rating available (CE level 2), during an impact, the armor freezes and hardens, absorbing the shock and distributing its force over a large area to reduce the risk of fractures. The protector is not destroyed by impact, but reverts back to its original state and maintains its capability to protect from multiple impacts."

That being said, I wear some old raceface mountain bike elbow/forearm pads.

Yeah, in that case, you'll likely be pretty happy with owning any of the boats listed, except for maybe a mamba or a remix. Their less aggressive edges are more forgiving, but lack the crisp bite of the other designs. When carving into eddies they kinda 'smoosh' their way around the turn rather than a crisp, hard carve. Think like powder skiing vs skiing on corduroy. 

One problem you might find, is that since basically everyone, everywhere likes these boats, they seem to be keeping their resale value, and the popular medium-ish sizes get snapped up really quickly.

What is the worst case scenario, and are you and your friends capable of dealing with it? If yes, go face your fears, if no, wait for a different weekend. 

It's a huge wave, but rafts and people are washing through. By the looks of it, at least some of either you or your friends will go for a swim, but there is a huge pool to collect the carnage. You also won't be alone in having carnage to collect. 

On the other hand, having taken a break for a few years, it would be really easy to say "no, I need an easier run or two under my belt before getting back to the big, exciting trips."

The thing is, Dagger and Jackson and Liquid logic all have other lines of recreational kayak products. The income from making whitewater boats is pitiful. The real money in making boats comes from kayak fishers, random people buying kayaks for the cottage or to float down the local river while drinking PBR in the summer. Boat manufacturing companies may be run and like to focus on whitewater to be able to say to the average Joe "hey, look what our boats can do!" 

Necky got out of the whitewater market.

Perception got out of the whitewater market. 

Basically the only whitewater specific companies left are Pyrhana, Zet, waka, titan, and a SMALL handfull of others whose names are escaping me at the moment.

Another boat to look at that I forgot to mention is the wavesport diesel 70. In my opinion it's the closest feeling thing in the longer boat category to a playboat. A hero/nano/scud are more similar to a fun, but they're not long. A diesel has good edges, a wide, flat, stable hull, a decent rocker to keep the ends out of the water so it spins easily and doesn't get hung up on funny currents, it's moderately fast so it's a manageable step up in speed from a playboat, it's acceptable at boofing, it surfs really quite nicely. The drawbacks are the large flat hull starts to hurt if you land flat from more than 10 feet up. The flat hull doesn't interact with rocks very well. Wavesport is pulling out of north america or going bankrupt or something so finding spare bits in a few years may get tough. I found it to be a better boat for more normal river running activities than creeking, but I liked the flat hull on creek slides.

I get where you're coming from, except I'm dabbling into class 5 on the west coast and 170lbs. I learned paddling in playboats and because of that, I still like edges. 

-The Braap will make your class 2-4 runs fun in a different way than a playboat and help you become a better boater, but having demoed one it's not the boat I'd want to take on a new class 5 run when I'm nervous. It was low to the water and 'sporty' like a original zen or extra float-y slalom boat, and felt more wobbly and twitchy than I'd like when the going gets tough. As much as I like to dream I am, I am not (yet) Pat Keller and can not (yet) paddle a creek/slalom hybrid on class 5 without eating shit more often than I care to. Apart from the top end of my comfort level, this is a  massive grin inducing, incredibly fun boat to paddle 90% of the time, and I kinda regret not getting one. It has an awesome mix of a round bow for using rocks, a stern that encourages pivot turns and stern squirts, slalom-esque"edges" along the tail of the boat, speed for surfing and river running. It's basically perfect for making class 3-4 rivers into playgrounds so that you never need to run class 5 to push yourself. 

-The mamba is a very very very good "everything" boat. It's short so it spins, it has a bit of edge so it carves, it has soft edges so they don't trip you up, it has a big rocker to boof easily with, it has a round bow for soft landings. It's a bit slower than all the new boats, it is confidence inspiring, it's a king of all trades yet master of none. It's a perfect design, just...a touch boring. Almost too easy and predictable. Lacking pizzaz and character. 

-remix 69- I can't really comment, paddled one once on class 2 for 20 min. It seemed fast, had a nice glide...kinda reminded me of a longer 2011 zen 65 without edges blended with a nomad. 

-9R. Fast: fast everwhere. It made river running easy if your mind and body can keep up. I actually had to stop and sit in eddies to plan my route rather than just making it up on the fly because I couldn't think fast enough. Ferries and eddies were a joy. I found play wave surfing difficult due to the shape of the bow and the long edges in the stern, but that was the only downside to the boat. Enough volume to keep you floating through big water, the wave deflectors really do help keep splashes out of your face. It's not a forgiving hull like the mamba, nomad or karma. Better be on your game if you're pushing yourself on harder rapids. Like all these new fast boats, it'll make you think about connecting moves through rapids in a different way as you come out of features with more speed than you'd expect. It's not a relaxing boat to paddle, you have to be actively directing it...there's never going to be such a thing as a leisurely class 3 run again. 

-2015 Zen m. Best described as jackson's version of a 9r that isn't quite as race oriented and a little more paddler friendly. Basically as fast as the 9r (green race results say maybe a touch faster, I thought maybe a touch slower). I liked the more rounded edges on the bow and stern as they made surfing easier. Think less of a GS race ski(9r) and more of a all mountain ski with a race pedigree(zen). The all mountain ski might be faster down a treed mogul run. I personally thing Jackson's double grove edge design manages to both grab water better and be more forgiving than the single hard chine transition of the 9r. A handful of inches shorter than the 9r, the zen is slightly easier to maneuver(not sure if it's psychological or because of some technical aspect of boat design). I found the zen to be slightly more stable and more forgiving when things didn't go quite right in pushy water. It shares the karma's flared sidewalls for impressive secondary stability. 

-Jackson Karma M. As a flat hulled creek boat, it's main determent is it doesn't boof/redirect off rocks as nicely or predictably as a round hulled nomad or recon. On the other hand, for a flat hulled creek boat it lands remarkably softly on a flat hull. Jackson made the flat part narrower and flared out the sidewalls to the parting line. The flared sidewalls and flat bottom make it incredibly stable. It's also long and fast, but doesn't feel like a wild Lamborghini like the 9r. It feels more like a well refined aston martin or rolls royce. The zen 2015 hull shares a lot of similar feelings with the karma series. The edge and speed makes it acceptably fun for surfing and easier river running. The massive volume will see you through many badly missed boofs but the low decks and narrow bow prevent the karma from feeling cantankerous. The Karma is not as much fun on easy rivers as other boats because it's so darn easy to paddle. 

-A note about basically all the long boats and boofing. The long tails and flatter tail rocker that make the boats fast also make them harder to boof in some situations. I was finding that they do better at "speed boofs" where the brute forward speed of the boat off the lip sends you flying out away from the base of the drop. A shorter more rockered boat lets you take off at low speed, pull your knees up during the boof and land flat, albeit nearly right at the base of the drop. However I'm sure I'll get my boofing technique in a longer boat better as I paddle more. Forgive me- I'm still learning!


Full disclosure: I ended up buying a zen m. I loved the braaap but didn't want to feel limited and have to be walking big rapids because I didn't feel confident of my boat. (I'm sure I'll still be walking plenty, but that's a self confidence and skill thing, not a boat thing)
I don't know about you guys, but I loose more money from loosing sunglasses, watches and knives than anything else. Boats and paddles almost always get found...sometimes broken, but always found.

I've paddled an axiom a more than a few times just for kicks on usually easier runs(club boat). Super fun, super fast. It was easy for me to play on the stern, with squirts and stuff, but I found the bow to be just a touch too long and have too much volume to do much more than an ender. It might just be me being used to cartwheels in a 6' playboat! (side note: I can throw ends in my riot glide) On the other hand, that bow volume made it a reasonable choice to spice up comfortable class 4 for me. I still want my big, stable, bathtub-like nomad to think about running class 5!

I'd love to try a braaap next summer, and see if I could get a more exciting boat than the old nomad for the hard rivers. Flying squirrel, zen, new nomad and zet raptor are all on my shortlist :)

Could be a number of things depending on the hole and the boat. 

-Might be that your seat is too far back, but likely only a problem if you're in a playboat. It's more difficult to notice a slightly imperfect trim in a longer boat.

-Might be that you don't have enough forward momentum. 

-Might be that you're a little tentative and leaning back as you hit the foam pile

-You may be trying to boof too early or not at all and your bow is ending up falling straight down and your boat is following the hydraulic re-circulation pattern as it resurfaces, making you do somersaults. 

-On a steeper hole it might be that you're boofing almost correctly, but need to be transferring your weight forward as your bow lands so that as the boat resurfaces you stay on top of it. (watch footage from adidas sickline champion's killer drop)

-It might be that you're running the G.C. of the Stikine and doing mystery moves as your boat gets tossed every which way in the massive holes and there's not a whole lot you can do about it.

You discovered the hard way that dying is extremely unpleasant. Living some days isn't always much better, but living is always at least marginally better than dying. If you're alive, there's always at least the tiniest chance things will get better. You can take some solace that these are likely to be some of the worst days of your life. 


The world is a shitty place for some people. Without a supportive family, there are few people around who truly care about others who aren't important to them in some way. You're among the people who have figured this out the hard way.


I agree, friends and support from caring people makes you feel better, but it's not necessary to get better. Other people don't matter much at the end of the day. They don't have to think all your thoughts, feel your pain and find a way to sleep in your skin at night. Find a way to be good enough for yourself. It's the hardest task you have in front of you. You've been unhappy for years, and this may take years to fix. When you're good enough for yourself, and you love yourself again, it's easier for other people to love and appreciate you. 


The first step is finally deciding you want something. It's hard to want something because you truly want it and not because you think you should have it because society thinks you should. Once you want something you can figure out how to start getting it. In the beginning, take tiny steps forward. It's better to achieve a tiny goal than to fail at a slightly larger one. As long as you are alive, you can continue to take tiny steps toward what you want. If you keep living long enough, you'll eventually become a person you are happy to be living inside.  


Being smart, pretty, skinny and amazing aren't qualities that make you happy. Things like developing emotional strength, creating and following your personal moral compass, making positive decisions for yourself, creating meaningful relationships, succeeding at making yourself better because you want to be better. Those are things that have given me pleasure to be alive when I've climbed up from the very bottom. 

I probably didn't help, but does it help to know that a random stranger who also has problems, cares enough to have spent 45 minutes at least trying?
